Coverage said the solid report could not overcome industry pessimism created by Lyft's weak outlook, while Uber's $5.9 billion GAAP loss from investment write-downs added to the negative headline.
UBER_2022q2.explicit_reasons: The clearest stated driver was Lyft's disappointing outlook and planned driver spending, which reaction articles said dragged Uber down despite its own revenue, adjusted-profit and outlook beats. FreightWaves also directly associated the early decline with losses on Uber's investments in Grab, Aurora and Didi.
UBER_2022q2.implicit_reasons: Uber's own quarter was mostly a counterweight: revenue of $6.85 billion beat the $6.13 billion consensus, adjusted EBITDA of $168 million beat $132 million expected, and second-quarter adjusted EBITDA guidance of $240 million to $270 million topped the $237 million average. Rider, trip and driver growth also showed recovery, but the market remained skeptical about sustainable profitability.

Guidance.text: Second-quarter adjusted EBITDA guidance of $240 million to $270 million exceeded the $237 million analyst average, and management expected meaningful positive cash flow for the year. The favorable outlook was presented as a counterweight rather than the cause of the selloff.

Revenue.text: Revenue of $6.85 billion exceeded the $6.13 billion consensus and rose 136% year over year. Coverage stressed that this beat was not enough to offset industry pessimism.

New Product Release / Users.text: Trips rose 18% and monthly active platform consumers reached 115 million, up 17% year over year, while the driver base reached a post-pandemic high. The articles gave no separate expectation for those user metrics and treated them as evidence of recovery.

Profits, costs and margin.text: Uber posted a $5.9 billion net loss, largely from $5.6 billion of investment-value declines, even as adjusted EBITDA beat expectations. FreightWaves directly linked the early share decline to those investment losses.

Macro and micro development.text: Lyft's below-consensus outlook and plan to spend more on driver incentives triggered pessimism across ride-hailing stocks. Several articles explicitly said Lyft's warning dragged Uber lower despite Uber's own solid report.

UBER_2023q4.summary_analysis: Uber reported third-quarter revenue of $9.29 billion and EPS of $0.10, both below consensus, but the shares recovered from an early drop and gained 3.7% in the session. Coverage explicitly credited above-consensus fourth-quarter bookings and adjusted-EBITDA guidance, healthy travel demand and accelerating profitability for overcoming the modest top- and bottom-line misses.
UBER_2023q4.explicit_reasons: The upbeat outlook drove the reversal. Uber forecast fourth-quarter gross bookings of $36.5 billion to $37.5 billion versus expectations around $36.31 billion to $36.5 billion and adjusted EBITDA of $1.18 billion to $1.24 billion versus $1.15 billion expected; Zacks directly said the shares gained on the upbeat outlook despite the misses.
UBER_2023q4.implicit_reasons: Quarterly revenue of $9.29 billion missed expectations of roughly $9.47 billion to $9.52 billion and EPS of $0.10 missed estimates of $0.12 to $0.13. Those negatives were offset by 21% bookings growth, a swing to net profit, expanding ride-hailing and delivery profitability, 15 million Uber One members and resilient travel demand.

Guidance.text: Fourth-quarter gross-bookings guidance of $36.5 billion to $37.5 billion was above expectations near $36.31 billion to $36.5 billion, while adjusted-EBITDA guidance of $1.18 billion to $1.24 billion topped the $1.15 billion estimate. Zacks explicitly tied the session gain to that upbeat outlook.

Revenue.text: Third-quarter revenue of $9.29 billion missed consensus estimates of roughly $9.47 billion to $9.52 billion. Coverage treated the shortfall as a negative that investors looked past in favor of bookings and guidance.

New Product Release / Users.text: Trips grew 25%, Uber One reached 15 million members and members spent four times more than nonmembers; the articles gave no separate expectation for those metrics. Coverage presented the engagement gains as evidence of platform strength.

Profits, costs and margin.text: EPS of $0.10 missed expectations of $0.12 to $0.13, but adjusted EBITDA reached $1.09 billion versus $1.02 billion expected and the company swung to net profit. Coverage emphasized the broader profitability improvement as outweighing the small EPS miss.

Macro and micro development.text: Resilient travel and return-to-office demand supported mobility growth despite inflation, while Lyft's price cuts had little apparent effect on Uber. The articles gave no quantified expectation for those conditions.

Immediate reaction divergence.text: Fox Business reported that Uber shares initially fell as much as 7% in premarket trading before recovering, while the project's two-day return finished in the opposite direction.

VZ_2022q4.summary_analysis: Verizon reported third-quarter adjusted EPS of $1.32 and revenue of $34.2 billion, both slightly above consensus, but its shares fell about 4.5% to 5%. Coverage explicitly said investors focused on weak subscriber growth: Verizon recorded 189,000 consumer postpaid phone losses and only 8,000 net postpaid phone additions overall versus more than 35,000 expected, while AT&T added 708,000.
VZ_2022q4.explicit_reasons: The subscriber shortfall was the first-order reason. Reaction articles said the shares fell as concern grew over waning customer growth, with only 8,000 postpaid phone additions versus more than 35,000 expected and substantial consumer losses after price increases.
VZ_2022q4.implicit_reasons: Revenue and EPS modestly beat estimates, but adjusted EBITDA declined 0.4% and the full-year outlook called for an adjusted-EBITDA decline of as much as 1.5%. Competition from AT&T and the apparent customer response to Verizon's pricing actions added to concerns.

Guidance.text: Verizon expected full-year adjusted EBITDA to decline by as much as 1.5%; the retained articles gave no separate consensus for that forecast. Coverage presented the outlook as reinforcing margin concerns.

Revenue.text: Revenue of $34.2 billion exceeded the roughly $33.8 billion consensus. Articles treated the beat as a positive that was outweighed by weak subscriber growth.

New Product Release / Users.text: Verizon added only 8,000 net postpaid phone subscribers versus more than 35,000 expected and lost 189,000 consumer postpaid phone users. Multiple reaction articles directly identified the subscriber shortfall as the reason shares fell.

Profits, costs and margin.text: Adjusted EPS of $1.32 beat estimates near $1.28 to $1.29, but adjusted EBITDA declined 0.4% to $12.2 billion. Coverage presented the deteriorating profitability metric as an additional concern.

Management.text: Recent pricing and fee increases were blamed for at least part of the consumer subscriber losses, while the articles gave no expectation for the effect of those actions. Coverage suggested the strategy had not yet strengthened the bottom line.

Macro and micro development.text: AT&T added 708,000 postpaid phone subscribers, making Verizon's weak additions look worse and heightening competitive concern. The articles did not state a prior expectation for AT&T's comparative impact.
